summary:
The shortest of Paul's letters, twenty-five verses, and the only private one: a single man, a single situation. Philemon is a believer in Colossae who hosts the church in his house. His slave Onesimus has somehow ended up with Paul in prison and become a believer there; Paul calls him "my child... whose father I became while I was in chains" (v. 10). Now Paul is sending him back, letter in hand. That backstory is essential — the letter never spells it out, and it is hard to follow without it.

Watch how Paul asks. He could command, and says so, but appeals instead: he puns on Onesimus's name, which means "useful" ("Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me," v. 11), offers to repay any debt in his own handwriting, and reminds Philemon, gently, that he owes Paul his very self. The request lands at verse 16: receive him back "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother."

Paul never condemns slavery as an institution here, a silence readers have wrestled with for centuries. What he does instead is collapse the distance the institution depends on: master and slave are now brothers, and Philemon must work out what that means in front of the whole church that meets in his home.
